reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Start
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 3, PostgreSQL in Action. In Module 2, we focused on how a relational database is organized. Now we start using that database by reading rows, filtering results, and making controlled changes. The main goal is not to memorize a long list of SQL commands. Instead, I want you to develop a safe working pattern: understand the question, write the smallest useful statement, run it, inspect the result, and verify any change before keeping it. Many slides include PostgreSQL code that runs directly in your browser. You can test the examples here first, then use Copy and paste the same SQL into the pgAdmin Query Tool for more practice. We will begin with SELECT and filtering, then move carefully into INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, transactions, and JSONB.

[tts-break]

Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, an analyst exploring operational records before building a report. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Big picture
slides.transcript:
Module 2 was mostly about structure: tables, keys, relationships, and constraints. Module 3 is where we begin interacting with the data inside that structure. When we only read data, a mistake may return the wrong rows. When we start changing data, a mistake can also modify or remove rows. That is why we will use a repeatable safety process. First, define what you need. Then preview the rows that match. Use a stable identifier when possible. Execute the smallest correct statement, and inspect what PostgreSQL returns. For write operations, verification is especially important. If you are not sure what an UPDATE or DELETE will touch, run a SELECT with the same condition first.

[tts-break]

Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, an application safely inserting or updating business records. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Learning path
slides.transcript:
We will approach SQL gradually. The first part is about reading data. You will use SELECT, choose columns, create aliases, apply filters, sort rows, and limit results. The second part is about changing data with INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE. Here we add stronger safety habits such as previewing target rows, using unique keys, and using RETURNING to see what changed. The third part is about protection and control. Transactions let us test changes and either keep them with COMMIT or undo them with ROLLBACK. The exercises follow the same progression. First run complete examples, then change one piece, then complete missing parts, and finally write short statements yourself.

[tts-break]

Focus on understanding the pattern before trying to memorize syntax. Connect this idea to a data engineer moving semi-structured API payloads into PostgreSQL. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Running case
slides.transcript:
Our running example is a small synthetic healthcare operations database. The patients table contains a medical record number, name, age, gender, and active status. Doctors contains a name and specialty. Admissions connects patients and doctors with diagnosis and admission information. Clinical notes stores some semi-structured information using PostgreSQL JSONB. The data is intentionally small so you can inspect the entire result and understand why a query returns particular rows. For teaching simplicity, the patients table stores age directly. In a real system, age is often calculated from a birth date for a particular reference date. As you work through the module, use these tables to practice the SQL idea rather than focusing on the healthcare domain itself. Connect this idea to an analyst exploring operational records before building a report. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it.

[tts-break]

After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: SQL language map
slides.transcript:
SQL commands are often grouped by the type of work they perform. DDL defines structure. Commands such as CREATE, ALTER, and DROP change the database schema. You saw much more of this in Module 2. DQL is commonly used to describe reading data, especially with SELECT. DML changes stored rows. INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes existing rows, DELETE removes rows, and newer PostgreSQL versions also support MERGE for synchronization patterns. Transaction-control commands decide whether a group of changes should be kept or undone. The labels are useful, but the practical idea is simpler: know whether your statement is only reading data, changing rows, changing structure, or controlling a transaction. That tells you how carefully you need to verify the result.

[tts-break]

When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as an application safely inserting or updating business records, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: SELECT pattern
slides.transcript: A SELECT query can be read almost like a sentence. SELECT tells PostgreSQL what columns or expressions should appear in the result. FROM tells it which table supplies the rows. WHERE can remove rows that do not meet a condition. ORDER BY controls presentation order, and LIMIT can keep only a chosen number of rows. You do not need every clause in every query. Start with the smallest version that answers the question. A good beginner habit is to list the columns you actually need. SELECT star is useful while exploring, but explicit columns make the result clearer and more predictable. Before writing a query, try saying the request in plain English. Then map each part of the sentence to the appropriate SQL clause. Think of SELECT work as progressively shaping a question. First identify the rows and columns you need, then filter, derive expressions, sort, and limit for inspection. A useful habit is to test each part on a small result before adding more complexity, especially when a filter contains NULL-sensitive logic.

slides.title: Run SELECT
slides.transcript:
Now let's run the first SELECT example. Before you select Run, read the query from top to bottom. Notice which columns are requested, which table supplies the data, and how the output is sorted. Run it directly in the browser and inspect the result table. Look at the column names and the row order. The query is not changing anything in the database. It is only creating a result from stored rows. Then make a connection between each clause and what you see. SELECT controls what appears as columns. FROM identifies the source table. ORDER BY changes the order in which the rows are displayed. If you want to practice in pgAdmin, copy the same query into the Query Tool and compare the result. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time.

[tts-break]

Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as an analyst exploring operational records before building a report, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Choose columns
slides.transcript:
This slide focuses on choosing only the columns you need. If a table contains many columns but the question only needs medical record number, patient name, and age, selecting those three columns makes the result easier to understand. Run the example and look at the output. Notice that the result is narrower than the full table. SELECT star is not wrong. It can be useful during exploration when you need to see the table structure. But in reports, applications, and reusable queries, explicit columns usually make your intent clearer. Also notice the sorting in this example. Before running it, predict who should appear first if the rows are sorted from the oldest patient to the youngest. Then compare your prediction with the result. Connect this idea to an application safely inserting or updating business records. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it.

[tts-break]

After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Aliases expressions
slides.transcript:
SELECT can return more than stored columns. It can also return expressions. An alias changes the label shown in the result. It does not rename the stored database column. An expression can calculate a new value for the result without changing the table. For example, you might derive a value from age or combine text into a more readable label. Run the example and inspect the output headings. Then compare them with the original table columns. The important distinction is between a result and stored data. A SELECT expression can make the output more useful while leaving the underlying table unchanged. If you run the same query in pgAdmin, notice that the alias appears as the result-column heading there as well. Connect this idea to a data engineer moving semi-structured API payloads into PostgreSQL. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it.

[tts-break]

After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: WHERE basics
slides.transcript: WHERE controls which source rows stay in the result. Different questions need different kinds of conditions. For direct comparisons, we can use equals, not equal, greater than, greater than or equal to, less than, or less than or equal to. BETWEEN is convenient for ranges. IN is useful when a value may belong to a short list. LIKE and PostgreSQL ILIKE support text patterns. Missing values need IS NULL or IS NOT NULL. We can also combine conditions with AND, OR, and NOT. A useful habit is to read the condition naturally. Age greater than or equal to sixty-five means sixty-five is included. When conditions become longer, use parentheses to make the intended grouping obvious rather than depending on memory of operator precedence. Think of SELECT work as progressively shaping a question. First identify the rows and columns you need, then filter, derive expressions, sort, and limit for inspection. A useful habit is to test each part on a small result before adding more complexity, especially when a filter contains NULL-sensitive logic.

slides.title: Change a filter
slides.transcript:
This example is designed to show how a small change in a condition changes the result. First, run the query exactly as shown and inspect which active patients meet the age requirement. Then change the age threshold from fifty to sixty and run it again. Before the second run, predict which rows should disappear. Notice that nothing is being updated in the patients table. We are only changing the predicate used to decide which rows appear in the SELECT result. This is one reason SELECT is a safe place to practice logic. You can adjust conditions and observe the effect without changing stored data. Try the same two versions in pgAdmin if you want additional practice comparing query results. Connect this idea to an application safely inserting or updating business records. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it.

[tts-break]

After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: BETWEEN and IN
slides.transcript: BETWEEN and IN are two readable filtering patterns. BETWEEN is helpful for a continuous range. When we say age between thirty and sixty, both endpoints are included. IN is useful when a column may match one of several listed values. Instead of writing several OR conditions, we can list the allowed values together. This example combines a range condition with a categorical condition. Before running it, read the WHERE clause in plain language and predict which records can qualify. Then run the query and compare the returned rows with your prediction. When a filter combines multiple conditions, check whether AND or OR matches the actual requirement. The SQL can be syntactically valid and still answer the wrong question if the logical connector is wrong. Think of SELECT work as progressively shaping a question. First identify the rows and columns you need, then filter, derive expressions, sort, and limit for inspection. A useful habit is to test each part on a small result before adding more complexity, especially when a filter contains NULL-sensitive logic.

slides.title: ILIKE
slides.transcript: PostgreSQL provides ILIKE for case-insensitive text pattern matching. The percent sign represents any sequence of characters. A pattern such as C followed by percent means starts with C. Percent followed by son means ends with son. Percent on both sides searches for text appearing anywhere inside the value. Run the example and look at the patient names that match. Then try changing the search pattern. Before each run, predict what kind of names should appear. ILIKE is useful when capitalization should not matter. LIKE is similar, but case behavior can differ depending on the database and collation. Pattern matching is convenient, but broad patterns can also return many rows. Use a pattern that reflects the actual search requirement. Think of SELECT work as progressively shaping a question. First identify the rows and columns you need, then filter, derive expressions, sort, and limit for inspection. A useful habit is to test each part on a small result before adding more complexity, especially when a filter contains NULL-sensitive logic.

slides.title: NULL
slides.transcript:
NULL represents missing or unknown information, and it does not behave like an ordinary value. A common beginner mistake is to write a condition that says a column equals NULL. That does not correctly test for missing information. Instead, use IS NULL when you want rows where a value is missing, and IS NOT NULL when you want rows where a value is present. In this example, a missing discharge date means the admission is still open. Run the query and inspect the rows that are returned. Look specifically at the discharge-date column. A simple way to remember this is that NULL is not a normal value such as zero or an empty string.

[tts-break]

It represents the absence of a known value, so SQL gives it special predicates. Connect this idea to an application safely inserting or updating business records. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Sort limit distinct
slides.transcript: Three common tools help organize query results. ORDER BY controls the row order. LIMIT keeps only a chosen number of result rows. DISTINCT removes repeated result rows. The important point is that LIMIT by itself does not mean latest, oldest, highest, or best. Without a deterministic ORDER BY, PostgreSQL is free to return any qualifying subset. Run the example that asks for the three most recent admissions. Notice that the date is sorted in descending order before the limit is applied. Now imagine removing ORDER BY. You may still get three rows, but you would no longer have a reliable reason to call them the three most recent. Use sorting to define what top or recent actually means before applying a limit. Think of SELECT work as progressively shaping a question. First identify the rows and columns you need, then filter, derive expressions, sort, and limit for inspection. A useful habit is to test each part on a small result before adding more complexity, especially when a filter contains NULL-sensitive logic.

slides.title: Logical order
slides.transcript:
SQL is written in one order, but it is useful to think about its logical processing in another order. For a simple query, PostgreSQL first identifies the source in FROM, then applies WHERE to filter rows. SELECT defines the result expressions. DISTINCT can remove repeated result rows. ORDER BY sorts the remaining result, and LIMIT keeps the requested number of rows. This mental model helps explain why filtering happens before sorting. It also helps explain why an alias created in SELECT is not always available in earlier logical stages. You do not need to memorize database-engine internals. Use this as a reasoning model. When a query behaves differently from what you expected, ask which stage creates or removes the value you are trying to use. Connect this idea to an analyst exploring operational records before building a report. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it.

[tts-break]

After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Complete a query
slides.transcript:
This slide gives you a small completion exercise. The query should return active patients who are age fifty or older. One comparison operator is missing. Before typing anything, translate the requirement into plain language. The age condition needs to include patients who are exactly fifty as well as those who are older. Replace the placeholder with the operator that expresses that idea, then run the query. Look at the result and verify that the boundary value would be handled correctly. This exercise is intentionally small. The goal is to connect one phrase in the requirement to one SQL operator, not to solve a long query all at once. You can use the browser editor and Run, then compare your output with the expected meaning.

[tts-break]

When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as an application safely inserting or updating business records, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: DML safety
slides.transcript: Now we move from reading data to changing stored rows, so our safety habits become more important. Before an UPDATE or DELETE, preview the target rows with SELECT. Use the same WHERE condition you intend to use in the write statement. Whenever possible, identify rows with a stable primary key or unique key rather than a name or other value that may repeat. A transaction can provide another layer of protection because you can inspect a change before deciding whether to keep it. RETURNING is also very useful in PostgreSQL because it immediately shows the rows that were inserted, updated, or deleted. The most important warning is simple: an UPDATE or DELETE without an appropriate WHERE clause can affect every row in the table. Writes deserve a slower workflow than reads. Before UPDATE or DELETE, run the intended WHERE condition as a SELECT and inspect the affected rows. In production, use transactions when appropriate so you can verify the change before committing. The absence of a syntax error does not mean the correct records were modified.

slides.title: INSERT
slides.transcript: INSERT adds new rows to a table. A good practice is to name the target columns explicitly. That makes it clear which value belongs to which field and makes the statement more resilient if the table structure later changes. PostgreSQL RETURNING can immediately show the row that was stored, including a generated primary key. Before running this example, look at the values and make sure the medical record number is unique and the age satisfies the table constraint. Then run it and inspect the returned row. If you copy the statement into pgAdmin, compare the returned values with a SELECT for the same unique key. INSERT changes stored data, so verification is now part of the workflow, not an optional extra step. Writes deserve a slower workflow than reads. Before UPDATE or DELETE, run the intended WHERE condition as a SELECT and inspect the affected rows. In production, use transactions when appropriate so you can verify the change before committing. The absence of a syntax error does not mean the correct records were modified.

slides.title: Complete INSERT
slides.transcript:
This exercise asks you to complete an INSERT for a new patient. Most of the statement is already provided. Your job is to supply a new unique medical record number in the missing location. Think first about the constraint. Medical record number is unique, so reusing an existing value should cause PostgreSQL to reject the insert. Enter a new quoted value, run the statement, and inspect what RETURNING shows. The exercise is not about memorizing the entire INSERT syntax. Focus on the relationship between the target column list and the values list. If an insert fails, read the error. A constraint error can be useful because it tells you the database is protecting a rule defined in the schema.

[tts-break]

When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as an application safely inserting or updating business records, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: UPDATE
slides.transcript: UPDATE changes values in rows that already exist. The safest pattern is to preview the intended target first. In this example, the SELECT and UPDATE use the same key-based condition. Run the cell and watch the sequence. First identify the row. Then change it. Finally inspect what PostgreSQL returns. A unique medical record number is safer than a patient name because names can repeat or change. When writing UPDATE, treat WHERE as a safety boundary. Before you execute, ask how many rows you expect the condition to match. If the answer is one row, but your preview SELECT returns several, stop and fix the predicate before running the update. This preview-then-update pattern is one of the most useful habits in practical SQL work. Writes deserve a slower workflow than reads. Before UPDATE or DELETE, run the intended WHERE condition as a SELECT and inspect the affected rows. In production, use transactions when appropriate so you can verify the change before committing. The absence of a syntax error does not mean the correct records were modified.

slides.title: DELETE
slides.transcript: DELETE physically removes rows, so we need to distinguish it from a soft-delete pattern. A soft delete keeps the row but changes a status field such as is active. That can preserve history while excluding the record from normal active views. A hard delete removes the row from the table. Run the soft-delete example and inspect the row after the change. Notice that the patient still exists but the active flag has changed. Whether a system should use soft or hard deletion depends on retention requirements, audit needs, and business rules. Before any hard delete, preview the exact target rows. Also remember that foreign-key constraints may block a deletion when related records depend on that row. Writes deserve a slower workflow than reads. Before UPDATE or DELETE, run the intended WHERE condition as a SELECT and inspect the affected rows. In production, use transactions when appropriate so you can verify the change before committing. The absence of a syntax error does not mean the correct records were modified.

slides.title: Constraints protect data
slides.transcript: This example intentionally triggers a foreign-key error. The patient we are trying to delete has a related admission. The database relationship uses a restrictive delete rule, so PostgreSQL refuses to remove the patient and leave the admission pointing to a missing record. Run the example and read the error message rather than treating it as a failure of the lesson. The database is enforcing a relationship rule that was designed in Module 2. This is an important change in perspective: not every error means your database is broken. A constraint error can be evidence that the database is successfully protecting data integrity. When you see this kind of error, ask which relationship or constraint is being protected before trying to bypass it. Constraints move important rules closer to the data. NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE, and foreign keys can stop invalid states before they spread into reports or applications. Application validation is useful, but database constraints provide a second line of defense shared by every client.

slides.title: Transactions
slides.transcript: Transactions let us group changes into a controlled unit of work. BEGIN starts the transaction. After that, changes are visible inside the transaction but have not yet been permanently kept. COMMIT keeps the changes. ROLLBACK discards them. In this example, we change a value, inspect the changed row, and then roll the transaction back. Before running it, note the original age. Then run the code and follow the output. You should see the temporary changed value, and after the rollback the final SELECT should show the original value again. This is a safe way to practice write statements. In pgAdmin, transactions are also useful when testing a change before deciding whether the result should be committed. Transactions let several statements behave as one logical unit. That matters when partial success would leave the database inconsistent—for example, creating an order header without its order lines or moving money out of one account without recording the corresponding destination. COMMIT confirms the unit; ROLLBACK abandons it.

slides.title: ACID
slides.transcript: ACID is a common way to describe important transaction properties. Atomicity means a related group of changes is treated as one unit. Either the intended transaction succeeds or its work can be undone. Consistency means database rules and constraints should still hold when a valid transaction finishes. Isolation deals with concurrent work so transactions do not incorrectly interfere with each other's intermediate states. Durability means that once a transaction is committed in a durable database system, the committed result is intended to persist even after failures. For this beginner module, the practical takeaway is not to memorize definitions word for word. Understand why transactions are useful: they give us a controlled boundary around related changes and a clear choice between keeping them and undoing them. Transactions let several statements behave as one logical unit. That matters when partial success would leave the database inconsistent—for example, creating an order header without its order lines or moving money out of one account without recording the corresponding destination. COMMIT confirms the unit; ROLLBACK abandons it.

slides.title: Write transaction
slides.transcript: Now you will write a short transaction using the earlier example as a pattern. The task is to change one patient age, inspect the changed row with RETURNING, then roll the transaction back. Start with the transaction boundary. Then write an UPDATE that targets the patient by the stable medical record number. Add RETURNING so you can inspect the temporary change. After that, undo the transaction and use a final SELECT to verify that the original value is back. Do not rush to copy a complete solution. Build the workflow one step at a time and run it when you think the sequence is correct. The goal is to understand the lifecycle: begin, change, inspect, undo, verify. Transactions let several statements behave as one logical unit. That matters when partial success would leave the database inconsistent—for example, creating an order header without its order lines or moving money out of one account without recording the corresponding destination. COMMIT confirms the unit; ROLLBACK abandons it.

slides.title: JSONB
slides.transcript: PostgreSQL JSONB lets a relational table store and query semi-structured JSON data. In the clinical notes table, the note column contains keys such as symptom, severity, and follow up. The arrow with two greater-than symbols extracts a JSON value as text. If the value needs to be compared as a Boolean or number, we may cast that text to the appropriate type. Run the example and inspect the symptom and severity columns that are extracted from the JSON document. The original JSONB column still exists as one stored value. The query is simply projecting selected keys into regular result columns. JSONB is useful when part of the data is flexible, but important relational identifiers and relationships should still be modeled deliberately. JSONB is useful when part of a record is genuinely flexible, such as an API payload or optional metadata. It should not become an excuse to hide well-understood relational fields inside one large document. A strong design keeps stable, frequently queried attributes relational and uses JSONB where flexibility adds real value.

slides.title: Complete JSONB
slides.transcript:
This exercise asks you to find notes that need follow-up. The JSON document contains a Boolean flag, but the key name is missing from the starter condition. Look at the earlier JSONB example and identify which key stores that follow-up information. Replace the placeholder with the quoted key name, then run the query. Inspect the returned notes and confirm that each one represents a true follow-up flag. Notice that extracting JSON as text is different from comparing a Boolean. The example handles that conversion for you. Focus on the pattern: choose the JSON key, extract the value, cast it when necessary, then use the result in a condition. You do not need to memorize every JSON operator yet. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time.

[tts-break]

Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as an analyst exploring operational records before building a report, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Insert select
slides.transcript: INSERT INTO followed by SELECT is a useful data-preparation pattern. Instead of typing individual VALUES, the SELECT query produces the rows that should be inserted into another table. This appears frequently in staging, ETL and ELT workflows, archives, reporting tables, and derived datasets. Run the example and inspect the newly created table containing patients in the requested age group. The important idea is that the SELECT controls which rows and columns move into the destination. Before using this pattern on larger data, verify the SELECT by itself first. Make sure it returns exactly the records you intend to insert. That follows the same safety principle we have used throughout the module: preview the result before performing the write operation. Think of SELECT work as progressively shaping a question. First identify the rows and columns you need, then filter, derive expressions, sort, and limit for inspection. A useful habit is to test each part on a small result before adding more complexity, especially when a filter contains NULL-sensitive logic.

slides.title: MERGE optional
slides.transcript:
MERGE is an optional advanced topic in this module. It can synchronize a source dataset with a target table. If a source record matches an existing target record, one action such as UPDATE can run. If there is no match, another action such as INSERT can run. The most important part is the matching condition because it defines what PostgreSQL considers the same record. If your browser engine supports the example, run it and inspect how matched and unmatched rows are handled. Do not worry if MERGE feels more complex than the earlier DML statements. The core skills are still SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and safe matching.

[tts-break]

Before using MERGE in important workflows, check for duplicate source keys and verify the match logic very carefully. Connect this idea to a data engineer moving semi-structured API payloads into PostgreSQL. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Common mistakes
slides.transcript:
This slide collects several mistakes that are easy to make when learning SQL. Use IS NULL rather than equality when testing missing values. When AND and OR appear together, add parentheses so the intended logic is visible. Do not use LIMIT to claim you have the top or latest rows unless ORDER BY defines what top or latest means. Avoid updating records by a name when a stable unique key is available. And before DELETE, preview the target rows with SELECT. These habits may look small, but they prevent large errors. When debugging, do not change many parts of the query at once. Read the requirement, identify the specific clause that is responsible, change one thing, run it again, and inspect what changed. Connect this idea to an analyst exploring operational records before building a report. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it.

[tts-break]

After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Guided practice 1
slides.transcript:
In the first guided practice, you will write two read-only queries. For Task A, return the requested patient columns and sort from oldest to youngest. Before writing the SQL, identify the selected columns and the sort direction. For Task B, keep only active patients who meet the age threshold, again sorted from oldest to youngest. Write the query in the browser and run it. Before checking the provided guidance, inspect your own result. For the reset dataset, think about which patient should appear first in the all-patient query and which patients should remain after the active-and-age filter. This is a good place to practice debugging because SELECT does not change the stored rows. Change one clause at a time and observe the result. For this activity, make a prediction before you run anything.

slides.title: Exercise 5 Transaction
slides.transcript:
Coding Exercise 5 combines an UPDATE with transaction control. You need to make a temporary age change, inspect it, roll it back, and then verify that the original value is restored. Think of the task as a sequence rather than one long statement. Start the transaction, make the targeted update, inspect the changed row, undo the transaction, and finally select the row again. Use Run and Check after the sequence is complete. The final verification is important. A successful rollback should leave the stored age at its original value. If the final value remains changed, review whether the rollback was executed inside the same transaction before the verification query. For this activity, make a prediction before you run anything.

slides.title: Final activity
slides.transcript:
The final activity asks you to combine the main ideas into one small PostgreSQL workflow. Begin with a SELECT using chosen columns, add a WHERE condition, and sort the result. Then insert one test row with RETURNING and verify that row with a key-based SELECT. After that, update the row safely. If you are ready for more, the optional challenge adds a transaction with ROLLBACK, a JSONB query, an INSERT INTO SELECT pattern, and an explanation of a constraint error. Do not try to do every part at once. Start from a pattern, change one piece, run it, inspect the result, and then add the next step.

That incremental method is how SQL work becomes easier to debug and safer to maintain. Connect this idea to a data engineer moving semi-structured API payloads into PostgreSQL. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Summary
slides.transcript: Let's summarize Module 3. SELECT defines the data you want to retrieve. WHERE and related predicates decide which rows qualify. ORDER BY, LIMIT, and DISTINCT help organize the result. INSERT adds rows. UPDATE changes rows. DELETE can remove rows. Because those commands change stored data, previewing targets and using stable keys are important safety habits. Constraints protect data rules and relationships. Transactions give you a boundary where changes can be committed or rolled back. RETURNING helps you inspect what PostgreSQL changed. JSONB extends PostgreSQL to semi-structured values, while INSERT INTO SELECT connects query results to data-preparation workflows. The habit to carry forward is simple: understand the request, preview the target, make the smallest correct change, inspect the result, and verify before you keep it. Do not treat this as a list to memorize. Try to explain each idea using one example from a project you understand. If you can describe when you would use the concept, what assumption it makes, and how you would validate the result, you are ready to apply it independently.
